en: BhG 12.1 Arjuna said:
Those devotees who, thus constantly disciplined, worship you with devotion;
And of those who [worship] the imperishable and unmanifest, which are the best knowers of yoga? (1)
Śrīdhara:
This twelfth chapter is undertaken to determine which is superior: the worship of the Nirguṇa (the qualityless) or the worship of the Saguna (the qualified).
At the end of the previous chapter, the excellence of one who is established in devotion was stated in the words, "Performing My work, regarding Me as the supreme" (Gītā 11.55).
Furthermore, through such passages as "O son of Kuntī, know this for certain" (Gītā 9.31), His very excellence has been determined here and there.

Likewise, through statements such as "Among them, the man of knowledge, ever-steadfast and single-mindedly devoted, is distinguished" (Gītā 7.17) and "By the boat of knowledge alone you shall cross over all evil" (Gītā 4.36), [His superiority is established].

And thus, the superiority of one established in knowledge has been stated. Even though both possess excellence, Arjuna spoke to the Blessed Lord with the desire to know the specific distinction, saying "Thus":

"Thus, those devotees who, being constantly disciplined through the offering of all actions and so forth, are established in You and worship You—the universal form, the omniscient, the omnipotent—meditating upon You."
And as for those who worship the imperishable Brahman, which is unmanifest and devoid of distinctions—among these two groups, who are the superior knowers of Yoga? This is the meaning. //1//
Madhusūdana said at the end of the previous chapter:
"O Pāṇḍava, he who performs my work, who regards me as the supreme goal, who is my devotee, who is free from attachment, and who is without enmity toward all beings— he comes to me."
Thus it has been said.

In that regard, there is a doubt concerning the meaning of the word "me" (*mad*): does the Blessed One refer by the word "me" to a reality that is entirely formless yet the source of all forms, or rather to one that possesses form?
For usage is observed in both senses.
"At the end of many births, the man of knowledge resorts to Me,
realizing that Vāsudeva is everything; such a great-souled one is very rare"—
in such passages as these, the formless reality is designated.
And immediately after the vision of the universal form:
"Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen Me. (Gītā 11.53)
Thus, the reality is with form (*sākāra*).

And since these two teachings of the Blessed One must be established according to the distinction between their respective qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*), otherwise there would be contradiction;

such being the case, I, who am desirous of liberation, must determine my own qualification as to whether the reality to be contemplated is indeed formless (*nirākāra*) or with form (*sākāra*), out of a desire to understand the specific difference between the meditations on the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) [Brahman].
Arjuna said: "So be it.

In this manner—according to the method just described in the verse beginning with "one who performs actions for Me" (Gītā 11.55)—those devotees who are constantly engaged, meaning they proceed with uninterrupted attentiveness toward the service of the Blessed One and so forth, being those who have taken sole refuge in the Reality that possesses form; remaining thus...

Those who constantly attend upon and meditate on you in such a form with its attributes, and those who are detached from everything and have abandoned all actions—they [attain] the Imperishable. It is called "Imperishable" (akṣara) because it does not perish and it pervades; this indeed is that Imperishable, O Gārgī, which the Brāhmaṇas declare to be neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long.
Brahman is devoid of all attributes (*nirguṇa*), with all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) prohibited by such scriptural passages as [BAU 3.8.9].
For this very reason, they worship You, who are unmanifest (*avyakta*), beyond the range of all the senses, and formless. Among these two groups, who are the best knowers of yoga (*yoga-vittama*)?
Both groups are indeed "knowers of yoga" (*yoga-vid*), for they either attain (*vindanti*) or know (*vidanti*) yoga, which is meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The meaning is: among them, who are the best yogis, and whose knowledge should I follow? //1//
Viśvanātha:
In the twelfth [chapter], it is stated that all devotees are superior to the knowers;
even among the devotees, those endowed with qualities such as freedom from hatred are praised.
At the beginning of the section on devotion (bhakti-prakaraṇa):
"Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me, full of faith—he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined. [Gītā 6.47]
Thus, just as the preeminence of devotion (*bhakti*) was established according to the Śruti,
so too, desiring to hear its preeminence even in the concluding summary, he asks:
"Those devotees who are thus ever-steadfast, who perform my work, and for whom I am the supreme goal" (Gītā 11.55)— these are the devotees characterized by what you have stated.

Those who worship You as the Śyāmasundara form, and those who worship the unmanifest, undifferentiated, and imperishable— this very imperishable which the Brāhmaṇas declare, O Gārgī, as described in such scriptural passages as "That Brahman is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long" (BAU 3.8.8)—
among both these groups of knowers of Yoga, who are the most excellent knowers of Yoga, and who know the supreme means for reaching You? Or rather, do they not attain it?

While they ought to be called "the most excellent among those who know yoga" (*yoga-vittama*), the expression "those who know yoga" (*yoga-vitta*) is used to convey the meaning: "among even many such as those who know yoga, who are the most excellent? //1//
Baladeva says:
"Among all means, pure devotion is of great power;
for it brings me [the goal] swiftly"—so Hari spoke in the twelfth [chapter].

Having known and realized the individual soul (jīvātman) as it truly is, one should meditate upon Hari, who is its part (aṃśin); this first path is described in the second chapter and those following through such passages as, "But know that to be indestructible" (Gītā 2.17). The second path is demonstrated in the seventh chapter and those following through such passages as, "O Pārtha, with the mind attached to Me" (Gītā 7.1), which teaches that only after knowing the individual soul to be a part of Hari should one meditate upon Hari, the possessor of that part, by means of devotion consisting of hearing about Him and so forth.
In those very verses beginning with "At the time of departure" (Gītā 8.10), devotion conjoined with yoga is described;
and by the verse "Others, too, through the sacrifice of knowledge" (Gītā 9.15), devotion conjoined with knowledge is stated.

Prior to the section on the six types of devotion, at the end of the sixth chapter, while about to teach unalloyed devotion, [the Lord] declared the supreme perfection of His own exclusive devotees through the verse beginning with "Of all yogis" (Gītā 6.47).
In this regard, Arjuna asks: "Thus" (*evam*).

"Those who, with their minds attached to me in the manner described by you in the passage beginning with *'O Pārtha, he whose mind is attached to me'* (Gītā 7.1), worship you, Śyāmasundara Kṛṣṇa, constantly engaged through all bodily and other activities," and so forth.

And those who worship the imperishable nature of the individual soul (jīva), which is unmanifest to the eyes and other senses, and who strive to realize it through concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi),
being seekers of the Supreme Self— among these two groups, who are the best knowers of yoga, those who employ the swiftest means? This is the underlying thought.
Some maintain that because meditation on Hari preceded by one's own direct experience is the root of liberation, through it the attainment of Him occurs without obstacles.

Others hold that since the formless and extremely subtle individual soul (jīvātman) is difficult to meditate upon, what is the use of such meditation? Rather, devotion to Hari alone is the crusher of all obstacles and the means to attaining Hari.
Since they are devoted to that very [path], ask them which of the two methods is the more excellent. //1//
The Blessed Lord said: Those who, fixing their minds on me, worship me with constant discipline;
Endowed with supreme faith, they are considered by Me to be the most disciplined. //2//
Śrīdhara: Regarding that, the Blessed Lord gave the reply "In Me" (mayi), meaning "the first are the best," to explain that those who have fixed their minds on Me—
the Supreme Lord— distinguished by qualities such as omniscience,
having made the mind one-pointed, [attain the highest goal].

Those who, being constantly disciplined through the performance of actions for My sake and so forth, are established in Me and worship Me with the highest faith—they are the most perfectly disciplined, and they are My favorite. //2//

Madhusūdana—Viśvanātha: Regarding this, he states that My devotees are the best: "In Me, who possesses the form of Śyāmasundara, having made [their minds] absorbed (āviṣṭa) by My entry (āveśya), they are ever-united (nitya-yuktāḥ), desiring constant union with Me, through supreme faith—that is, faith transcending the qualities (guṇātītayā). As it has been said:
"Faith directed toward the self is characterized by *sattva*; faith in ritual action is characterized by *rajas*;
the faith of the *tāmasa* person is in unrighteousness; but faith in service to Me is beyond the *guṇas*. (BhP 11.25.27).
Thus, "those who are mine"—meaning my own exclusive devotees—are the most disciplined, the best among those who know yoga. This is the meaning.
By this, the meaning is made manifest that others who possess devotion mixed with knowledge, action, and so forth, are inferior to those who are single-mindedly devoted;
and thus it is established that devotion is superior to knowledge, and within devotion, single-minded devotion is superior. //2//

Baladeva: Thus questioned, the Blessed One said, "In Me. Those devotees who, having fixed their minds upon Me—the Supreme Lord, the son of Devakī, whose attributes include being dark-complexioned like a blue lotus—and having made them steadfast, endowed with supreme and firm faith, worship Me as described by these characteristics.

Those who perform worship of Me characterized by hearing and so forth, being ever-steadfast and constantly desiring union with Me—they, by My own reckoning, are considered the most disciplined; they are those who employ the means for quickly attaining Me. //2//
But those who worship the Indestructible, the indefinable, the unmanifest,
all-pervading, unthinkable, immovable, stable, and eternal; (3)
Having fully restrained the collection of the senses and possessing a mind that is equal toward all things, those who delight in the welfare of all beings attain Me alone. //4//
Śrīdhara: If that is so, why then are the others not superior?
To this he says, "But those who... in two verses.
The connection between the two [verses] is as follows: "But those who worship the Imperishable, who meditate upon it—they too attain Me alone."
"The characteristic of the syllable (akṣara) is indefinable," and so forth. "Indefinable" means it cannot be defined by words, because it is unmanifest and devoid of form and other such qualities.
It is all-pervading and omnipresent;
it is inconceivable precisely because of its unmanifest nature;
it is immutably fixed, abiding as the substratum within the "peak" (kūṭa) of the phenomenal expansion of māyā.
"Immovable" means free from vibration;
for that very reason, it is "fixed," meaning eternal and devoid of growth and so forth.
The rest is clear. //3-4//

Madhusūdana: In response to the inquiry—"What is the superiority of those who know the Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma-vid) over those who know the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahma-vid), by virtue of which you consider only the former to be 'perfected souls' (yuktātman)?"—he introduces those who characterize that superiority, namely the knowers of the attributeless Brahman, with the two verses beginning "But those... (ye tu).
The connection with the second [verse] is as follows: "Those who worship me as the Imperishable (akṣara) also attain me alone.
The word *tu* is used to highlight the distinction from the previous [worshippers].
The "Imperishable" is the undifferentiated Brahman well-known in the *Vācaknavī-brāhmaṇa*; there are seven qualifiers for the purpose of defining it.

It is "indescribable" (anirdeśya), meaning it cannot be designated by words, because it is unmanifest; for since there is no distinction [in the unmanifest], the application of words is impossible. Why is it devoid of genus (*jāti*) and so forth? To this he says: "all-pervading" (*sarvatraga*), "all-encompassing" (*sarvavyāpin*), and "the cause of all.
Therefore, it is empty of genus and the rest, because the connection with genus and so forth is observed only in the case of limited effects.
Furthermore, because even space and so forth are admitted to be effects,
it is for this very reason inconceivable; it is not an object of mental activity, just as it is not an object of verbal activity, since that too has only delimited objects.
Since there is the Vedic scripture stating, "From which words turn back,
together with the mind, having failed to reach it," how then [can one say], "I ask you about that person who is known through the Upaniṣads"?
The scripture states, "But it is seen by the highest intellect," and there is also the aphorism, "Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source.

It is replied: through a connection imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*), when the final modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) produced by sound [i.e., the Veda] takes the form of the realization of supreme bliss...
Since it is possible for ignorance and its effects—which are superimposed—to cease when they are reflected upon a pure object, the term "object" is used figuratively.
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that the connection with ignorance is merely superimposed upon that [pure Self], he says: "unchanging" (kūṭastham).

That which is false yet perceived as true is called "fraudulent" (kūṭa) by people in the world, as in expressions such as "a fraudulent kārṣāpaṇa coin" or "false testimony. Likewise, ignorance— known as *māyā*— together with the manifold expansion of its effects, although false, is [perceived] by worldly people as true.
The term *kūṭastha* means that which stands as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) through a superimpositional relationship (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*) with respect to the superimposed (*pratīyamāna*) peak;
the meaning is that it is the substrate of ignorance and its effects.
By this, all logical inconsistencies are resolved.

It has been established. Therefore, since all modifications are imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*), the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*) which is their substrate is changeless; thus he says "immovable" (*acalam*), meaning free from movement or modification.

Precisely because it is immovable, it is "fixed" (*dhruvam*), meaning unchanging and eternal. Such pure Brahman they worship me, having dispelled through hearing (*śravaṇa*) any impossibility regarding the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And by means of reflection (*manana*), immediately thereafter, for the sake of ceasing contrary mental impressions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*), they meditate upon the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

The meaning is that they take it as their objective through meditation known as "contemplative absorption" (*nididhyāsana*), which consists of a continuous flow of identical cognitions—like a stream of oil—by setting aside heterogeneous cognitions. //3//

But how, when there is contact between the sense objects and the senses, can heterogeneous cognitions be set aside? To this he says: "having restrained [them] from their respective objects," that is, having withdrawn the collection of senses, the aggregate of instruments;
by this, the perfection of tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth, is expressed.
Since the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for the enjoyment of objects exists, from what cause would the senses turn away from them? To this he says: "in every object."

Those whose minds are even— equal with respect to joy and sorrow, and free from attachment and aversion— because ignorance, which is the cause of those states, has been removed by right knowledge, and because longing for sense objects has been discarded through the practice of perceiving their defects,
they are "even-minded" in all circumstances.
By this, the detachment characterized by mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā-vairāgya*) has been described.

Therefore, because they are free from hatred—the cause of violence—due to the absence of the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) everywhere, they are devoted to the welfare of all beings. Having performed the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), they have bestowed the gift of fearlessness upon all beings with the mantra: "I grant fearlessness to all beings; may it be well."

Thus, according to the Smṛti, "Having granted fearlessness to all beings, one should practice renunciation. Being such as this, endowed with all the means of perfection and having themselves become Brahman, they attain Me— the imperishable Brahman itself— through a doubtless direct realization that constitutes the fruit of all spiritual disciplines.
The meaning is that even previously they were of my very nature, and by the cessation of ignorance, they remain as my very nature;
for so it is stated in such scriptural passages as, "Being Brahman, one attains Brahman," and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
And here too it has been stated: "But the man of knowledge is My very Self; this is My opinion" (Gītā 7.14). //3-4//

Viśvanātha: But those who worship my own nature as the non-differentiated Brahman are inferior to that [state] because they are subject to suffering; thus he says in two verses beginning with "But those... The Imperishable (akṣaram) is Brahman, which cannot be designated by any word because it is unmanifest (avyaktam), being devoid of form and other such qualities.
All-pervading, it extends through all places;
inconceivable, it is beyond the reach of logic;
immutably stable, it pervades all time.
According to Amara, that which pervades time by virtue of its single form is "immutable" (kūṭastha);
it is "immovable" (acalam), meaning devoid of increase and so forth,
and "constant" (dhruvam), meaning eternal.
"Only me"—because there is no difference between that syllable and me. //3-4//
Baladeva: But for those who do not perform my worship preceded by the direct realization of their own self, there will indeed be attainment of Me;
however, because it occurs with extreme hardship and after a very long time, they are inferior to them [the former]. He says this in three verses beginning with "But those who...
Those who first worship the imperishable, which is the consciousness of one's own self—
The connection is that their affliction is greater.
He qualifies the Imperishable (akṣara): it is "indescribable," meaning it cannot be designated by words such as "god" or "human" which denote the body, because it is distinct from the body;
it is "unmanifest" (avyakta), being beyond the range of the eyes and other senses; and it is "all-pervading" (pratyak sarvatraga), permeating the body, the senses, and the vital breaths.

Inconceivable, beyond the reach of logic, and knowable through scripture alone; its very nature is knowledge, and its very nature is the knower; it is immovable, being devoid of motion because it is of the nature of knowledge;
it is fixed, remaining forever stable in its state of being the sole remainder for the Supreme Self.
He states the injunction for the meditation on the Imperishable with the words "having fully restrained."

Having fully restrained the group of instruments— the collection of senses such as hearing— and having withdrawn them from their activities, which consist in the movement toward sound and other objects,
they possess an even-mindedness, an equal vision, toward all— whether friends, allies, noble persons, or neutral parties;
or rather, those beings whose intellect is fixed upon the same Brahman abiding in all things, whether sentient or insentient.

Those who are devoted to the welfare and benefit of all, striving appropriately with the thought, "May there be well-being for everyone," and who thus engage in devotion to Me— which is characterized by the dedication of one's actions and preceded by the direct realization of the Self—
they too undoubtedly attain Me alone, whose primary nature is supreme sovereignty. //3-4//
For those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest, the difficulty is greater;
for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with hardship by those who possess bodies. (12.5)

Śrīdhara: Now, if they too attain You alone, then from what [source] does the state of being "most appropriate" for others arise? In response to this expectation, He states the distinction created by affliction (*kleśa*) and non-affliction in three verses, beginning with "Affliction":
For those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest—the undifferentiated Imperishable (*akṣara*)—their affliction is greater.

For indeed, because the goal or final attainment (*gati*) which has the Unmanifest as its object is reached with as much difficulty by those who identify with the body as [the attainment of] suffering itself.
Because it is difficult for those who identify with the body to constantly incline toward the inward [Self]. //5//
Madhusūdana: Now, demonstrating the superiority of these [latter] over the former, he says "kleśa" (affliction).

Even for the former, there is indeed greater affliction in withdrawing the mind from sense objects and fixing it upon the Saguna Brahman, as well as in being constantly devoted to that practice and endowed with supreme faith;

however, for those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest—the ones intent on contemplating the Nirguna Brahman and possessing the aforementioned means—their affliction, their exertion, is *adhikataraḥ*, meaning exceedingly or more intensely great.

On this point, the Blessed One himself states the reason: "The goal is indeed unmanifest. For the goal to be reached—the Brahman which is of the nature of the Imperishable and constitutes the fruit—is attained by those possessing bodies (dehavadbhiḥ), that is, by those who identify with the body, only through great hardship. Having renounced all ritual actions and approached a teacher, there is a great effort required in the investigation of the Vedāntic texts through various means to dispel each respective delusion.
Therefore, it has been said that their affliction is even greater because it is established by direct perception;
for although the fruit is indeed one and the same, the intention is that those who attain it through difficult means are superior. //5//
Viśvanātha: If that is so, in what respect do they possess inferiority? To this he says, "affliction" (*kleśa*).

It is called the "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) because it is not manifested by anything at all; for those whose minds are attached to that very Brahman and who desire to experience it, there is a greater affliction in reaching its goal.

For indeed, since the path to the Unmanifest cannot be made manifest by any means, that goal is attained by embodied beings (*dehavat*—i.e., living souls) only with as much difficulty as if it were a state of suffering.
For indeed, the capacity of the sense organs consists only in the specific cognition of sound and so forth,
and not in the cognition of anything beyond that.
Therefore, for those who desire a cognition devoid of such distinctions, the cessation of the sense organs is necessarily required.
But the cessation of the senses is indeed as difficult as the stopping of the current of rivers;
as was said by Sanatkumāra:
"By devotion to the playful grace of the petals of whose lotus feet..."
The virtuous untie the knotted accumulation of karma;
likewise, even ascetics whose intellects are not yet purified and who have merely blocked the flow of the senses cannot do so. Therefore, resort to that Vāsudeva, who is free from all conflict.
In this world, those without a boat desire to cross the great ocean of existence, where the sixfold group of senses acts as crocodiles, by means other than happiness;
therefore, you should worship the feet of the Blessed Lord Hari.
"Having made a raft, cross over the difficult-to-traverse ocean of calamity.
Even if that goal is attained through such great hardship,
it is nevertheless attained only by means mixed with devotion.
However, for those who worship Brahman alone without devotion to the Blessed One, there is only the acquisition of pure affliction and not the attainment of Brahman;
as was said by Brahmā:
"For them, only affliction remains."
"It is not otherwise, like those who thresh coarse husks," [BhP 10.14.4]. //5//
Baladeva: But if they too should attain You alone, then on what basis is the state of being "most fit" attributed to the former [devotees]?
To this he says: *kleśo 'dhika* ("the affliction is greater").

For those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest—their intellects intent on meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon the extremely subtle and formless individual soul (*jīvātman*)—their affliction is more intense.

Although even for those of the past, the practice of devotion to Me without attachment and the withdrawal of the senses from objects other than Me certainly involve hardship, nevertheless, because of the manifestation of Me, whose very form is bliss, it does not appear as a hardship.
How much less, then, could there be any question of its being more difficult? It is utterly cast aside.
For this reason, the unmanifest goal—the mental state directed toward the unmanifest Imperishable—is attained with great difficulty by embodied beings, that is, by people who identify with the body.

The sense is: since those possessed of bodies have for a very long time habitually regarded only the gross body as the Self, how could they possibly succeed in habitually regarding the subtle consciousness—which has long abandoned self-reflection—as the Self?
As for what they explain here:
Brahman is of two forms, with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa).
Among these, meditation on the qualified [Brahman] is easier and less prone to error because its object possesses a formal shape.
However, the worship of the attributeless (nirguṇa) is painful and prone to error because of the absence of its true nature.

That attributeless Brahman is expressed by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable). For the realization of its state beyond attributes, there are seven qualifiers: it is indefinable and beyond the scope of the Vedas.
Because it is unmanifest, devoid of birth and so forth;
all-pervading, omnipresent;
and inconceivable, inaccessible even to the mind.
And scripture says: "From which speech, along with the mind, turns back without reaching it" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1), and so forth.
The world, though unreal and illusory, is called a "kūṭa" because it appears as if real, just like a counterfeit kārṣāpaṇa coin or the like.
In that [Brahman], it exists as the substrate through the relation of superimposition;
therefore, it is non-transient, changeless, firm, and eternal.

Indeed, for those who know it, there is great hardship consisting of approaching a guru, followed by inquiry into the Upaniṣads, reflection on their meaning, and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*) upon them.

For the former [liberated souls], however, liberation— characterized by identity with the attributeless, imperishable Self which constitutes the very nature of the Lord— occurs through a higher knowledge (vijñāna) that arises solely from the grace of the Lord as taught by their Guru, and which destroys ignorance along with its effects, even without those [rituals]. Thus, although the fruit is the same,
there is a distinction of inferiority and superiority based on the presence or absence of afflictions (kleśa).
This [objection] is weak because of the commonality of their movement; for in the Sūtra, the dual nature of Brahman is refuted by the statement,
"as that Imperishable is attained," since its being known through the Vedas is heard there,
and because the passage beginning with "whence words turn back" intends to mean that it is not within the scope of the senses in their entirety.

Because it lacks any basis for linguistic application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*), that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) cannot be an object of valid cognition; nor can it be the "thing to be defined" (*lakṣya*), because it is accepted as being expressible by all words. Furthermore, since an entity that exists eternally in a single state is designated as "immutable" (*kūṭastha*), the world is not immutable.
For in passages such as, "The Seer, the Wise One, the All-pervading, the Self-existent, has ordained all things according to their true nature for eternal years" (Īśopaniṣad 8),
his reality is heard.

Because, upon hearing of the supreme Brahmanhood of the Lord whose conscious form is nursed at Yaśodā’s breast, the conceptualization of an attributeless, imperishable reality residing within Him is merely a product of intellectual dullness. //5//
But those who, having renounced all actions unto Me, are intent on Me, worshiping Me by practicing yoga with undivided devotion while meditating upon Me; 6.
I am the deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence for those whose minds are absorbed in Me; I become so, O Pārtha, before long. (7)
Śrīdhara: He says in two verses beginning with "But those who... that for My devotees, however, perfection is attained without effort simply through My grace.
Those who, having renounced—that is, surrendered—all actions unto Me, the Supreme Lord, become intent on Me and meditate upon Me.

The meaning is: "By means of undivided [devotion] (ananya)" refers to that by which no other object worthy of worship exists; one should worship Him through the yoga of exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti-yoga). //6//
"Of them" means: for those by whom their minds have been thus absorbed in Me, I shall quickly become their perfect deliverer from the ocean of saṃsāra, which is joined with death. //7//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: Surely, when the fruit is identical, excellence and inferiority would arise from the smallness or greatness of the afflictions (*kleśa*); but that very thing does not exist here. For the fruit for those who know the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*) is the state of being Brahman—which is non-differentiated supreme bliss and consciousness—through the cessation of ignorance and its effects.

However, for those who know the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahma*), because there is no sublation of the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna-pramā*), there is no cessation of ignorance; thus, the fruit for those who have gone to the world of the effected Brahman (*kārya-brahma-loka*) is a particular divine sovereignty (*aiśvarya-viśeṣa*).
If it is argued that, for the sake of a greater fruit, an increase in effort does not result in a deficiency [of the means], we say no;

for those whose all obstructions have been dispelled by the meditation on the *saguṇa* [Brahman], true knowledge arises spontaneously through the Vedāntic texts— assisted by the grace of the Lord— without the teacher’s instruction and without the labor of repeated hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), thereby bringing about the cessation of ignorance and its effects.

For it is established that at the conclusion of the enjoyment of sovereignty in the Brahma-world itself, there arises the supreme liberation which is the fruit of the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman;

according to the Śruti: "He beholds the Puruṣa, dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings. Thus, having attained the sovereignty of Hiraṇyagarbha, at the end of his enjoyment, he [beholds] beyond this "mass of living beings" (jīva-ghana), which is the collective totality of all individual souls.

He beholds— that is, directly realizes through the authority of the Vedanta which has manifested within himself— the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is beyond the most excellent Hiranyagarbha, who is distinct from him, yet superior and dwelling in the city (the body), seated in the cave of one's own heart, the full Purusha, non-different from the inner self (pratyag-ātman), and without a second.
The meaning is that one becomes liberated by that much alone.

And thus, even without the previously mentioned afflictions, those who know the Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma) attain the fruit of the knowledge of the Brahman without attributes (nirguṇa-brahma-vidyā) through the grace of the Lord; this point is stated in the two verses beginning with "But those who...
The word "but" (tu) is intended to remove the aforementioned doubt.

Those who, having renounced all actions and surrendered them to me, Vāsudeva, who possesses attributes, and being thus *mat-parāḥ*— meaning those for whom I, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva alone, am the supreme and most excellent object of affection— remain through *ananya-yoga* alone; that is,
through a yoga or meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which has no other support than me, the Blessed Lord, and which is otherwise known by the name *ekānta-bhakti-yoga*.

[Visualize] me, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the treasury of the essence of all beauty, whose form is a mass of bliss, having two or four arms; either filling the flute—which enchants the minds of all people—with the seven notes so enchanting to the ear, or with sprout-like hands resting upon a lotus bud, the Kaumodakī mace, and the discus; or in the forms of Narasiṃha, Rāghava, and others.

Or else, meditating upon My universal form as it has been shown, they worship Me— that is, they maintain an uninterrupted flow of mental states in a uniform manner, or they remain in close proximity to Me; for those whose minds are absorbed in Me— meaning those by whom the mind has been focused and entered into Me with one-pointed concentration— I, the Blessed Lord, am constantly worshipped by them.

I shall soon—very quickly—become the deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence; that which is called "worldly existence" (saṃsāra) consists of death along with the manifold expansion of false knowledge and its effects, and it is like an ocean because it is difficult to cross. I shall become the one who lifts [beings] out of it, properly and without effort, and the one who establishes them above all afflictions in the pure Brahman, which has overcome all obstacles, by granting the support of knowledge.
"In that very birth"; the address "O Pārtha" is for the purpose of providing consolation. //6-7//

Viśvanātha: He says "But those who... to show that for devotees, liberation from the cycle of existence occurs easily through devotion alone, even without knowledge. "In me" means having renounced—that is, having abandoned—all things for the sake of the ultimate goal; for the word *saṃnyāsa* here has the meaning of "renunciation" (*tyāga*).

"By yoga alone" means by the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) which is indeed devoid of knowledge, ritual action, austerity, and so forth, as it was said: "Whatever is attained by ritual actions, whatever by austerity, and whatever by knowledge and dispassion... (BhP 11.20.32).
Immediately following this:
"By the yoga of devotion to Me, My devotee easily attains everything—
both heaven and liberation, as well as My own abode— if he so desires" (BhP 11.20.33).

If it is asked, "But what is the method for their crossing over saṃsāra?"—it is true that no inquiry regarding the method for their crossing over saṃsāra is even known. Therefore, he says "of them," implying: "I myself shall deliver them, even without such a method."
Thus, the implication is that the Blessed One has affection only for his devotees, and not for the men of knowledge. //6-7//

Baladeva: Having thus heard the true nature of the self, those who practice exclusive devotion (*kevalā bhakti*) toward Me—the Self who am the possessor of parts—and do not strive for the direct realization of the self, for them, the attainment of Me shall occur in no time at all through My exclusive devotion alone; this He declares in the two verses beginning with "But those... (*ye tu*).

Those who are my exclusive devotees (*mad-ekāntinaḥ*), having renounced all their own prescribed duties for the sake of attaining me— abandoning them with the understanding that they would distract from devotion— and being intent on me alone with me as their sole goal of life, worship me, Kṛṣṇa, by means of the yoga characterized solely by hearing about me and so forth, which is without any other [object].
They perform that worship characterized by Me, meditating upon Me even at the time of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, with their minds fixed on Me.

For those devotees whose consciousness is absorbed in Me and whose minds are exclusively attached to Me, I alone am the deliverer from the ocean-like cycle of existence joined with death, which is difficult to cross.
Without delay—that is, with haste, unable to endure any postponement in attaining them—I place them upon the shoulder of Garuḍa and lead them to My own abode.
"I cause them to attain"— this means their attainment of my abode is independent of the path beginning with light; "I lead them to the supreme station without the journey through light and so forth,
having placed them upon the shoulders of Garuḍa, going wherever I wish, unhindered."

Thus, according to the words of the Vārāha Purāṇa: "Even devotion independent of ritual action and the like is the means for accomplishing one's desired goal— that which is indeed the perfection of the means for the four aims of human life."
Without her, a man who takes refuge in Nārāyaṇa attains that [state].
Thus it is said in the Nārāyaṇīya:
"Even all righteous people do not attain that destination which those who are free from all dharmas and who utter only the name of Viṣṇu reach with ease."
And thus from the Padma [Purāṇa]. //6-7//
Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me. Thereafter, you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt. (12.8)
Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore [the Lord says], "in Me alone.
Place—that is, make firm—the mind, which consists of volition and doubt, in Me alone.
Also, settle the intellect, which is characterized by resolve, in Me alone.

Acting thus, having obtained knowledge through my grace, from this point forward, at the end of the body, you shall dwell in me alone; you will reside there, where you yourself shall make your abode. Of this there is no doubt.
And as the Śruti says: "At the end of the body, the Divine reveals the supreme Brahman, the Savior. //8//

Madhusūdana: Thus, having praised the meditation upon Brahman with attributes (*saguṇopāsanā*) through this extensive discourse, he now enjoins it with the words "in Me alone" (*mayy eva*). Place—that is, establish—the mind, which consists of volition and doubt, in Me alone, the Brahman with attributes; make all mental fluctuations have Me as their sole object.
By the application of the word "alone" (*eva*), place the intellect, characterized by determination, in Me alone.
Make all modifications of the intellect have Me alone as their object;
the meaning is: by abandoning other objects, contemplate Me at all times.

To the question "What will happen from that?", He says: "You shall dwell"—that is, you shall abide—having attained knowledge, with Me as your Self, in Me alone, the Pure. Henceforth, at the end of this body, there is no doubt; there is no suspicion of any obstacle here.
The meaning is "it must be performed.
Thus, in the phrase "from this point forward" (*eva ata ūrdhvam*), the absence of the euphonic conjunction (*sandhi*) is for the sake of completing the verse. //8//

Viśvanātha: Since devotion to Me alone is supreme, He instructs him to practice that very devotion through three verses beginning with "In Me alone. By the use of the particle *eva* ("alone"), the exclusion of the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*) is intended.
The meaning is: "Fix your mind on Me—the dark-beautiful one, clad in yellow garments, and wearing a forest garland; that is to say, perform the remembrance of Me."
Likewise, "establish your intellect in discernment" means: perform reflection upon Me.
And that reflection consists of the repeated study of the scriptural passages that set forth meditation.
And from that, "you shall dwell in Me alone"—this is a Vedic usage.
The meaning is that you have attained a dwelling in my very presence. //8//
Baladeva said: Since this is so, therefore you should fix your mind on me alone, and not on your own self; compose it and make it concentrated. Place your intellect in me, entrust it to me.
Acting in this way, you shall dwell in me alone, that is, in my very presence as Kṛṣṇa.
But the meaning is not that you will attain Me, who am preeminent in sovereignty, while experiencing creation and so forth like one who possesses a fixed abode. //8//
But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me, then seek to reach Me, O Dhanañjaya, by the yoga of practice. 12.9

Śrīdhara: Here, he states an easy method for one who is incapable [of the previous practice], beginning with "Now" (atha). If you are not able to fix the mind upon Me in such a way that it becomes steady, then, having repeatedly withdrawn the distracted mind, desire to attain Me through that yoga of practice characterized by the constant remembrance of Me.
Exert yourself! //9//

Madhusūdana: Now, with three verses beginning with "atha," [the Lord] prescribes three means for those who are unable to meditate on Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma), according to the degrees of their incapacity: first, the practice of meditation on the Lord externally through an image and so forth; if that is impossible, the performance of the duties of a devotee (bhāgavata-dharma); and if that is impossible, the renunciation of the fruits of all actions.

Now, if you are unable to fix and establish the mind upon me so that it remains steady for the duration of a watch (pakṣa), then—having withdrawn the mind from all other objects and concentrated it upon a single focal point such as an image—practice the repeated fixing of the mind;
yoga is preceded by that practice, which is samādhi. Through that yoga of practice, strive to attain Me.
"O Dhanañjaya!

Having conquered many external enemies, you have brought back wealth; now, having conquered the single enemy that is the mind, you will bring back the wealth of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*)—this is not surprising for you. This is the meaning of the address, according to Viśvanātha. He states "Now" (*atha*) as the means for attaining that [knowledge] for one who is unable to remember it directly.
Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the repeated withdrawal of the mind—even when it has wandered here and there—and its stabilization once again upon my very form;
that itself is *yoga*, by means of which [one proceeds].

Because of its natural tendency toward the base forms, tastes, and so forth, one must restrain the movement of the river of the mind as it flows toward them, and gradually direct that movement toward my exceedingly beautiful form, taste, and so forth.
The meaning is "accomplish.
O Dhanañjaya! The sense is that since you have brought back wealth after conquering many enemies, it is certainly possible for you to grasp the wealth of meditation by conquering even the mind. //9//

Baladeva: If it be objected, "Surely for those whose mental fluctuations are restrained like the Ganges, the attainment of You would be swift; but since my mental fluctuation is not such, how can that [attainment] be mine?"—to this He says: "But if... (atha). If you are unable to fix or offer the mind upon Me steadily and with ease, then seek to attain Me through the yoga of practice; strive for that.

The sense is this: having withdrawn the mind that has wandered elsewhere, its gradual stabilization upon Me is "practice" (*abhyāsa*); when the mind becomes inclined toward Me through that practice, the attainment of Me will become easy.
(BhG 12.10) "If you are unable even in practice, be intent on My work."
Even while performing actions for my sake, you shall attain perfection. //10//
Śrīdhara: If, however, it is not thus, he says "abhyāsa" (practice).

If, moreover, you are unable even to practice, then become one for whom the supreme [duty] is the performance of those actions intended for my pleasure—such as the vow of fasting on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), ritual service, worship, and the chanting of My names.
Even by performing such actions for My sake, you shall attain liberation. //10//

Madhusūdana: "For the sake of pleasing Me, perform *mat-karma*—the duties of a devotee (*bhāgavata-dharma*) such as hearing and chanting—and be intent upon that alone, being devoted exclusively to it. If you are unable to practice this fully, even while performing those actions known as *bhāgavata-dharma* for My sake, you will attain perfection characterized by the state of Brahman, by way of the purification of the mind and the arising of knowledge.
Viśvanātha: Regarding the phrase "even in practice": it is like a tongue corrupted by bile which does not desire sugar-candy.

The meaning is: if you think, "In the same way, the mind corrupted by ignorance does not perceive even that which is sweet, such as those forms and so forth; therefore, I am simply unable to fight with that exceedingly powerful mind which is so difficult to grasp.
[He is one] for whom my actions are supreme.

By performing my rites—such as hearing, chanting, bowing, worshiping, sweeping my temple, sprinkling water, gathering flowers, and other forms of service—one shall attain perfection characterized by becoming a beloved attendant, even without the constant remembrance of Me. //10//
Baladeva: If you object, "Since the mind is as excessively fickle as the wind, I lack the power for its withdrawal (pratyāhāra)," he says in response: "Even in practice" (abhyāse 'pi).
If you are incapable even of practice characterized as previously described, then become one whose supreme actions are dedicated to Me—that is, those which constitute the ultimate human goal.
And these have been mentioned before: the construction of My temple, the watering of My flower gardens, and so forth.

Thus, while performing these easily accomplished actions for my sake, you—by virtue of the greatness of my form, which is exceedingly beautiful to behold—will have your mind fixed upon me in such a way that you shall attain perfection characterized by proximity to me; therefore, this means is extremely easy to follow. 10.
But if you are unable even to do this, then, taking refuge in my yoga, renounce the fruits of all actions with a self-controlled mind. (12.11)
Śrīdhara: With the word "atha" (now), he states an alternative for one who is utterly incapable of being firmly established in the dharma of the Lord.

If you are unable to do even this, then, having resorted to *mad-yoga*—that is, taking me alone as your sole refuge—and having become steady-minded, renounce the fruits of all necessary actions, both those performed for visible and invisible purposes, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and others.
This is what is being said: "I have already stated that, by the command of the Lord, actions must be performed according to one's capacity.

As for the fruit—whether seen or unseen—it is dependent upon the Supreme Lord alone. Thus, having placed the burden upon Me and abandoned attachment to the results, you shall, through My grace, achieve your purpose, O Madhusūdana. Now, if because your mind is drawn toward external objects you are unable even to be intent on these actions dedicated to Me, [then listen to this:]

Therefore, having resorted to my yoga—which is the state of taking refuge in me alone—and having resorted to that yoga which consists of the dedication of all actions to me, being self-controlled (meaning one whose senses are restrained) and possessed of self (meaning one who is discerning), perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions; the meaning is: abandon the desire for results. //11//
Viśvanātha: If one is unable to do even this, then, having resorted to my yoga, one should offer all actions unto me.
Having resorted to that yoga of mine, perform the renunciation of the fruits of all actions as described in the first six chapters.
This is the meaning: in the first six chapters, it was stated that the yoga of selfless action (niṣkāma-karma-yoga) offered to the Lord alone is the means to liberation.
In this second hexad, bhakti-yoga alone is declared to be the means for attaining the Blessed One.
And that bhakti-yoga is twofold: the internal mental activity centered on the Blessed One, and the external sensory activity.

In this regard, the first [type] is threefold: consisting of recollection, consisting of reflection, and, for those who are unable to maintain uninterrupted recollection, that which takes the form of repeated practice toward that [object] by those who are attached to it. This triad alone is difficult to traverse for those of dull intellect; however, for those of keen intellect who are free from fault, it is indeed easy to traverse.
The second [set], however, consisting of hearing and chanting, is indeed an easy means for everyone.
Thus, those qualified persons who possess both means are declared in this second hexad to be superior in every respect.

O Blessed One, those who are capable of this task—those who have reached steadfastness in the Lord, yet remain devoid of faith, and who perform desireless actions dedicated to the Lord—are the qualified candidates for the first six verses; we, however, are indeed inferior to them. //11//

Baladeva said: "Now, if you are unable to perform even those very easy acts that please Me— such as sweeping My temple and so forth— because you are hindered by obstacles such as being born of a noble family or being a leader of the world,
then, having taken refuge in My yoga, which is My shelter, [dedicate] all the actions you are performing."

Being self-controlled and having conquered the mind, perform the renunciation of fruits; likewise, through actions such as the *agnihotra*, *darśa*, and *paurṇamāsa* sacrifices— which are forms of worshiping Me and are devoid of attachment to results—
by means of knowledge that has arisen within like a thread of poison, [realize] the relationship of subordinate and principal between yourself and the Supreme Self.
"When one's own master has arisen and is known to be the most excellent of all, supreme devotion toward him will gradually arise.
He will say exactly this later with the words beginning "From whom the activity of beings [proceeds]" up to "one attains supreme devotion to Me" (18.55–56). //11//

Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is superior to knowledge; the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation; and from renunciation, peace follows immediately. (12.12)
Śrīdhara: He praises this renunciation of fruits with the words "the better" (śreyaḥ).
Knowledge preceded by instruction accompanied by reasoning is superior to practice devoid of right knowledge;
even more distinguished than that is meditation preceded by such [knowledge].
For it is stated in the Śruti: "Then one beholds that partless [Self] while meditating.
Therefore, the renunciation of the fruits of action characterized as described above is superior.
From such renunciation of the fruits of action, through the cessation of attachment to actions and their results, and by My grace, the stilling of saṃsāra occurs immediately thereafter. //12//

Madhusūdana: Now, by concluding the exposition of the means right here, He praises this renunciation of all fruits with the words "The better" (*śreyaḥ*). Knowledge is indeed more excellent—that is, the ascertainment of the Self through both scripture and reasoning. Meditation (*dhyāna*), known as *nididhyāsana*, is superior to knowledge—that is, to the hearing and reflection perfected by the practice of listening for the sake of knowledge—because it is the immediate cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). It excels because it is the proximate cause for that realization.

Thus, having established that meditation (*dhyāna*) is the best of all means of accomplishment, the renunciation of the fruits of action performed by the ignorant is praised as being even superior to that.
It follows [from the context] that "the renunciation of the fruits of action is distinguished from meditation.

From the renunciation of the fruits of all actions performed by a person whose mind is fixed, peace—that is, cessation—of *saṃsāra* along with its causes occurs immediately thereafter through focused attention, and not after some other time.
It depends on this:
"When all desires that dwell in his heart are utterly released, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman."

From such scriptural passages as "When one renounces all desires," and from the definitions of the one of steady wisdom (*sthita-prajña*) such as "he who has abandoned all desires," it is understood that the renunciation of all desires is the means to attain immortality.

Furthermore, since desires are the fruits of action, the renunciation of those [fruits] is praised by way of its commonality with the renunciation of desire, just as the fruit of renouncing all desires;
for example, it is said that "the ocean was drunk by the Brahmin Agastya."

Or, just as the earth was made devoid of Kṣatriyas by the Brāhmaṇa Jāmadagnya, and because of that commonality of being Brāhmaṇas, even contemporary Brāhmaṇas are praised for their immeasurable prowess—so it is with Viśvanātha. Having thus clarified the superiority of the aforementioned remembrance, reflection, and practice in their respective order, He says: "For better than... [Śreyo hi]. Reflection upon Me—which was stated as "fix your intellect on Me"—is better, that is, more excellent, than mere practice. This is because knowledge arises from practice, and it has been said, "I shall place your intellect in Me. Thus, reflection upon Me is superior.

When there is practice, meditation (*dhyāna*) would occur only through effort; however, when there is reflection (*manana*), meditation occurs without effort—this is the distinction. Therefore, meditation is superior even to knowledge; the meaning is that it is more excellent.

Why? To this he says: from meditation comes the renunciation—that is, the absence of longing—for the fruits of action such as the happiness of heaven, as well as for liberation, which is the fruit of desireless action.
Even though that [liberation] is obtained by itself, there is indifference toward it;
however, prior to unwavering meditation, those devotees who have not yet developed [spiritual] delight would still possess a desire to abandon liberation.
But for those possessing unwavering meditation, there is indifference toward liberation.
That very [devotion] is what brings about the lightness of liberation.
As it is said in the *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*: "It destroys affliction and bestows auspiciousness" (BRS 1.1.7); here, its majesty is celebrated through these six words. As it has been stated:
Neither the station of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra,
nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the realms of taste;
neither the perfections of yoga nor even liberation from rebirth.
"One whose self is offered unto Me desires nothing other than Me" (BhP 11.14.14).
"One whose self is offered unto Me" means one who is steadfast in meditation upon Me.
From renunciation, or rather from dispassion, immediately follows peace: the cessation of the senses with respect to all sense-objects, except for My own form, qualities, and so forth.

It should be noted here that because the two words *śreyaḥ* and *iti* in the first half-verse are construed with [the following], whereas in the second half-verse they are construed only with *anantaram*, this very interpretation is correctly established and no other. //12//

Baladeva: Because it is easy to perform, because it is free from negligence, and because it contains knowledge within it, [the Lord] praises Karma-yoga as having an unintended fruit with the words "For [Karma-yoga] is better," etc.

Knowledge—consisting of the direct realization of one's own Self—is better (more excellent) than practice, which consists of the continuity of remembrance of Me, even when that practice is unperfected;

this is because knowledge serves as the door to the perception of the Supreme Self. And compared to that unperfected knowledge, which is still a means, meditation characterized by reflection on one's own Self is distinguished as being more beneficial for one's welfare.

And from that meditation which is not yet perfected, immediately after the renunciation of the fruit of action, there is peace; the meaning is that mental purity is established immediately after the action whose fruit has been relinquished.
And thus, when the mind is pure, meditation is perfected;
when meditation is perfected, there arises knowledge in the form of direct personal realization.
When knowledge is perfected, there arises the knowledge of the Supreme Self, which is its fruit.
Through that, supreme devotion is attained—my attainment as the Lord characterized by sovereignty; thus, the sense is that this means is difficult to traverse.
Furthermore, this is not an instruction intended for Arjuna alone.
Because of his single-minded devotion,

those who are established in goodness, who delight in desireless action, and who meditate upon Hari, experience their own self; thereafter, through supreme devotion— which has arisen from that [experience], which is directed toward Hari, and which possesses the quality of supreme sovereignty— they experience Hari as the object of their love.
"Are liberated"—this is the sequence of the meaning of the Gītā scripture; however, it should be understood as referring to one who is devoted to exclusive dedication (*ekāntitva*). //12//
One who is not hateful toward any living beings, who is friendly and compassionate, free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, equal in pleasure and pain, and patient— (13)
The yogi who is always contented, self-controlled, and firm in resolve;
whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me. 14.
Śrīdhara: With eight verses beginning with "adveṣṭā," [the Lord] declares the qualities that cause the swift grace of the Supreme Lord for such a devotee:
one who is free from hatred toward all beings as they are, friendly, and compassionate; specifically, one who is devoid of hatred toward those who are superior.
One who behaves with friendliness toward equals is "friendly" (*maitra*);
the meaning is that one is compassionate toward those who are inferior.
Because of that very compassion, one is without the sense of "mine" and without egoism; such a person is one for whom pain and pleasure are the same as those of others.
Patient and of a patient disposition. //13//
"Contented" means always contented in both gain and loss, with a mind that is perfectly serene;
the yogi is vigilant, self-restrained, and of a disciplined nature.
He whose devotion to my domain is firm,
by whom mind and intellect are offered unto Me—
such a devotee of Mine is dear to Me. (14)

Madhusūdana: Thus, having prescribed the worship of the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman—which is easy to perform—by censuring the worship of the Imperishable (akṣara) as being exceedingly difficult for a dull-witted candidate, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva has, in accordance with the gradations of incapacity, prescribed other means as well; [now he explains] how indeed one might become free from all obstacles through the state of being a supreme candidate.

This is because the prescription of the means is for the sake of the fruit, with the intention that one should enter into the imperishable knowledge (*akṣara-vidyā*) which constitutes that fruit. As it has been said: "Those who are dull-witted and unable to directly realize the supreme Brahman devoid of distinctions are shown compassion through descriptions of [Brahman] with distinctions."

"When their minds have been brought under control through the practice of saguṇa-brahman, that very [Brahman] itself shall manifest directly, free from the conceptualization of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Thus it was said by the venerable Patañjali: "The perfection of samādhi arises from devotion to the Lord (īśvara-praṇidhāna)."
"Then there is the attainment of inward consciousness as well as the absence of obstacles. The word "then" (tataḥ) means "from the devotion to Īśvara.
Thus, this censure of the meditation on the syllable [Oṃ] is for the purpose of praising the meditation on the qualified [Brahman], and not because it is to be abandoned.
Just as in the injunction for the *udita-homa* (sacrifice after sunrise) there is a deprecation of the *anudita-homa* (sacrifice before sunrise),
according to the maxim that "a deprecation does not function to deprecate the deprecated thing, but rather to praise the enjoined thing," therefore,
it is only those who meditate upon the syllable (*akṣara*) who are, in the ultimate sense, the best among the knowers of Yoga.
"For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me.
All these [others] are indeed noble, but the knower, in My view, is My very Self" (Gītā 7.17–18).
Since they have been repeatedly described as being most praiseworthy by such passages, it is their knowledge and their entire collection of dharmas that should be followed.

Desiring to awaken Arjuna by means of his specific qualification (*adhikāra*), the Blessed One, who seeks the supreme welfare of others, praises those who perceive non-duality and have accomplished their task—the worshippers of the Imperishable—through seven verses beginning with "adveṣṭā.

Seeing all beings as the Self, one does not hate them because of the absence of a contrary perception even toward that which causes one's own suffering; rather, such a person possesses friendliness and affection for all beings.
Because he is compassionate—compassion being pity for those who suffer—he possesses that [quality] and is thus a giver of fearlessness to all beings; this is the meaning of "paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka.
He is "without the sense of 'mine'" (nirmama), being devoid of the notion of "mine" even with respect to his body.
He is "without egoism" (nirahaṅkāra), having emerged from the egoism produced by conduct, Vedic study, and so forth.
He for whom pleasure and pain are equal because he does not give rise to hatred or attachment;
therefore, being patient, he does not undergo any transformation of mind even through verbal abuse, physical assault, and the like. //13//
There are further qualifiers for that very person:
"contented" means being satisfied whether there is gain or loss of the causes for maintaining the body, having conceived the notion of "enough";
likewise, whether there is gain of things possessing qualities or the opposite.

The word "constantly" (*satatam*) is connected to every [term]. The "yogi" is one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhita-citta*). "Self-restrained" (*yatātmā*) means one whose aggregate of body, senses, and so forth is fully controlled (*saṃyata*).

"Of firm conviction" means one whose resolve is steady and cannot be overcome by fallacious reasoners; his determination is: "I am the non-agent, non-enjoyer, Brahman who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss and without a second. This is the meaning of "one of steady wisdom.
"With mind and intellect dedicated to Me"—that is, with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) surrendered to Me, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the pure Brahman.
Such a devotee of Mine, who knows the pure Imperishable Brahman, is dear to Me, because he has My very Self as his essence. //14//

Viśvanātha: In response to the question of what kind of devotee becomes such through this peace (*śānti*), he describes the differences in the natures of various types of devotees in eight verses beginning with "adveṣṭā" (one who is non-hating).

"Adveṣṭā" means one who does not harbor hatred even toward those who hate him; on the contrary, he behaves as a friend, being a "mitra" by virtue of his friendship. He is "karuṇa," compassionate toward them with the thought, "May they not fall into an evil state."
Now, one might ask: by what kind of discernment (*viveka*) can friendliness and compassion arise even toward enemies?

To this he replies that it is "without discernment," meaning that because such a devotee of Mine is free from the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) regarding children, wife, and so forth, and is free from the sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṅkāra*) regarding the body, hatred never bears fruit for him anywhere at all.
The sense is: how much more so, then, must he embrace solitude for the sake of pacifying the suffering born of hatred?
Now, one might object: "But even in that state, some physical pain surely occurs due to kicks, blows with the fist, and so forth, inflicted by others?
To this he replies: "Equal in suffering and happiness."
As it was said by the Blessed One, whose crest-jewel is the half-moon:
"All those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa do not fear anything from any quarter;
they regard heaven, liberation, and hell as equal in their purpose. [BhP 6.17.28]
Equanimity toward pleasure and pain is the state of seeing them as equal.
And that [equanimity] consists of the contemplation: "This is the fruit of my past actions (*prārabdha*); it must necessarily be experienced.
Even in the midst of equanimity, it is only through endurance that suffering is borne; thus he says "the patient one" (*kṣamī*), meaning one who possesses forbearance.
The verbal root *kṣam* means "to endure.
[An objection is raised: "But how can the livelihood of such a devotee be secured?
To this he replies: "He is contented (*santuṣṭaḥ*)."
He is content with whatever food is available, whether it comes by chance or through effort.
Now, it has been said that he is "equal in pain and pleasure";

how then can he be described as being "content" upon seeing his own food? To this, he replies: "The yogi is always [intent on this] because he is joined to the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*), for the sake of attaining perfection in devotion"—this is the sense. As it has been said:
"It is indeed proper for one who strives for the sake of food to sustain life;
for by means of that [food], reality is investigated, and having realized that, one may go to the Supreme.
Furthermore, even if he does not obtain alms due to fate, he remains self-restrained—meaning his mind is controlled and free from agitation.

It is said that even when a disturbance of the mind occurs by chance, one does not at all practice the eightfold yoga and so forth for the sake of its pacification; the meaning is that his firm resolve—that "unswerving devotion alone must be practiced by me"—does not waver.
The reason for this in every respect is that his mind and intellect are offered unto Me; the meaning is that he is solely intent upon remembering and contemplating Me.
The meaning is: "Such a devotee is dear to me, for he brings me exceeding joy. (13-14)

Baladeva: Having thus described the steadfast and other types of single-minded devotees, as well as the non-exclusive devotees and those who possess a formal commitment through their various respective means, [the Lord] now sets forth the qualities that attract them all in seven verses beginning with "adveṣṭā. He is "one who does not hate" any living beings; even toward those who harbor hatred, he is free from malice, perceiving: "These [beings], impelled by the Supreme Lord who acts in accordance with my own will, are hating me. Thus, he is devoid of hatred.
Thinking, "These are the manifestations of the Supreme Lord," he is friendly and affectionate toward them;
thinking, "May there be no distress for these beings who are distressed by some cause," he is compassionate;
and being free from the sense of "mine" regarding the body and so forth—thinking, "These are the transformations of primordial nature (prakṛti), not mine"—he is devoid of possessiveness toward them.
Free from egoism, he is devoid of the conceit of self regarding those [objects].
Equal in pain and pleasure, he is undisturbed by joy when there is happiness or by agitation when there is suffering. For this reason, he is patient, enduring each and every thing.
Constantly contented in both gain and loss, with a serene mind,
the yogin is devoted to the means taught by the guru;
self-controlled, he has conquered the host of his senses.

One who possesses firm resolve—that is, one whose determination that "I am the servant of Hari" is stable and cannot be overcome by fallacious reasoning—and who has thus dedicated both mind and intellect to Me;
such a devotee of Mine is dear to Me, for he brings Me joy. (13–14)
He from whom the world does not tremble, and who does not tremble from the world; he who is free from joy, envy, fear, and agitation—he is dear to Me. 12.15
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "from whom" means from whose presence people—the world—do not tremble, do not suffer agitation through fear or apprehension;
and who does not tremble before the worlds.
And he who is endowed with natural joy and the rest:
therein, joy is enthusiasm upon obtaining what is desired for oneself;
indignation is intolerance toward the gain of another.
Fear is dread;
agitation is the disturbance of the mind caused by fear and the like.
My devotee who is free from these is dear to Me. //15//
Madhusūdana: Furthermore, there are further qualifications of that very person, beginning with "because":
because no person whatsoever in the world is agitated or distressed on account of that renunciant who bestows fearlessness upon all beings;
and likewise, he who is not himself agitated by wicked people, for whose sole vow is the non-disturbance of those who have done him no wrong.
This is because he possesses the vision of non-duality (advaita), is supremely compassionate, and is by nature forgiving.

Furthermore, joy (harṣa) is a particular modification of the mind that manifests bliss and causes physical reactions such as horripilation and the shedding of tears upon obtaining something dear to oneself.
Resentment (amarṣa) is a particular modification of the mind characterized by an inability to endure the excellence of others.

Fear (*bhaya*) is a particular modification of the mental state dependent upon the sight of tigers and the like; terror (*trāsa*) is a particular modification of the mental state in the form of agitation, such as "How shall I live alone in a desolate place, devoid of all possessions? He is one who is free from those [states]—joy, impatience, fear, and terror.

The meaning is that he has been abandoned by those very people themselves because they are unfit for it due to their adherence to the doctrine of non-duality (advaita), and not because I have personally exerted myself to cause their abandonment.
By this, the phrase "my devotee" is drawn back [from the previous verse].
Such a devotee of mine as this is dear to me, as stated before. //15//

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, as stated in such passages as, "In one who possesses unalloyed devotion to the Blessed Lord, all the gods reside through all their virtues" (BhP 5.18.12), other virtues that produce my pleasure also arise spontaneously through devotion to me when it has been repeatedly practiced.
He says, "Listen to those as well," by means of five verses beginning with "Because...

He speaks again of certain qualities—such as being free from worldly joy and so forth, namely joy, resentment, fear, and agitation—as previously mentioned, in order to make known their rarity, starting with the verse: "He who does not rejoice... (15).
Baladeva: Because no person in the world is agitated by fear of him, nor does he experience disturbance;
because, out of compassion, he performs no action that would distress people;
and because he is not agitated by the world, since it is certain that he is non-opposed to all, the world performs no action that would distress him.
And he who is liberated from joy and the other [emotions] as their agents, yet does not himself engage in their liberation—
this means that because he is immersed in an exceedingly profound self-delight, he is devoid of even contact with them.
In this context, joy (*harṣa*) is the enthusiasm for the acquisition of what one possesses; indignation (*amarṣa*) is the inability to endure the acquisition of what belongs to another;
and fear (*bhaya*) is the state of being terrified, dependent upon the sight of a malevolent being.
The agitation of thinking, "How can there be life for me who am devoid of effort," is *udvega* (distress).
These are the four fluctuations of the mind. //15//
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, free from distress, and who has renounced all undertakings— that devotee of mine is dear to me. (12.16)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the term "anapekṣaḥ" (independent):
one who is independent is free from longing even for an object that has presented itself by chance.
"Pure" (śuciḥ) means one who is endowed with both external and internal purity.
Dakṣa means diligent;
udāsīna means free from partiality;
gata-vyatha means devoid of mental anguish.
He whose nature it is to renounce all undertakings and exertions for both seen and unseen purposes—he who is My devotee in such a state is dear to Me. //16//
Madhusūdana: Furthermore, "independent" (anapekṣa) means one who is indifferent toward all objects of enjoyment, even when they are brought to him by chance;
"pure" (śuci) means one endowed with both external and internal purity.
Dakṣa is one who, when matters to be known or actions to be performed have arisen, is immediately capable of knowing and acting.
He is indifferent, meaning he does not take the side of anyone, such as a friend or the like.
He is free from distress (*gatavyatha*), meaning that even when struck by others, no distress or pain has arisen in him.

Forgiveness (*kṣamitvam*) is the state of not retaliating even when suffering has arisen; it is the distinction between the non-arising of suffering despite the presence of its causes, and the absence of suffering once it has already passed. My devotee who is a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), whose nature it is to abandon all actions and all undertakings—whether their fruits pertain to this world or the next—is dear to Me.
Viśvanātha: "Independent" (anapekṣaḥ) means devoid of expectation regarding worldly activities; "indifferent" (udāsīnaḥ) means unattached to worldly affairs.
He is one whose nature it is to abandon all worldly undertakings—whether for visible or invisible purposes—as well as certain ultimate pursuits such as teaching the scriptures and so forth. //16//
Baladeva is independent; he is free from desire even for objects of enjoyment that come to him spontaneously.
He is pure, possessing both external and internal sanctity.
He is skillful, being capable of investigating the meaning of his own scriptures.

Indifferent means not grasping at the positions of others; free from distress means being devoid of mental anguish even when harmed; one who has renounced all undertakings is one who is devoid of every effort directed against his own devotion. //16//
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires, who has renounced both the auspicious and the inauspicious, and who is full of devotion— he is dear to Me. 17.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "he who"—
meaning he who does not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant,
and he who does not feel aversion upon encountering what is unpleasant.
He is one who does not grieve when a desired object is lost;
he who does not long for an object not yet attained;
and whose character it is to relinquish both the auspicious and the inauspicious, merit and demerit.
Having become thus, he who possesses devotion to me is dear to me. //17//
Madhusūdana: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he who," he explains this [by the term] "equal in pain and pleasure": he who does not rejoice upon obtaining what is desired;

He does not feel aversion upon encountering the undesirable, nor does he grieve when what is desired is lost; he does not long for the attainment of the unattained. This explains the phrase "one who has renounced all undertakings": one whose nature it is to renounce both auspicious and inauspicious actions—that is, those actions which are the means to happiness and the means to suffering—is "one who has renounced the auspicious and the inauspicious," and such a person is "possessed of devotion."
He who is dear to me. //17//
Viśvanātha: Nothing.
Baladeva: He who, upon obtaining a beloved son, disciple, or the like, does not rejoice;
and upon encountering that which is unpleasant, does not feel aversion toward it.
When that beloved object has perished, he does not grieve;
he does not long for what has not been attained.
He is one whose character is such that he is disposed to renounce both the auspicious merit and the inauspicious evil, because both are equal in their nature as obstacles [to liberation]. //17//

He who is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor; who is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and who is free from attachment—[that yogi is dear to Me]. (18)
To whom blame and praise are equal, who is silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion—such a person is dear to Me. (19)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "equal" means being of one and the same form toward both enemy and friend;
likewise, he is exactly the same even in the face of honor and dishonor.
The meaning is that he is devoid of joy and dejection;
he is the same toward cold and heat, and toward pleasure and pain; he is free from attachment, being unattached to anything whatsoever. //18//
Furthermore, "equal in censure and praise" means one for whom censure and praise are equal;
he is a sage, restrained in speech.
Content with whatever is obtained by any means whatsoever;
homeless, being devoid of a fixed dwelling;
steady-minded, with a settled heart.
The man who is thus constituted and possessed of devotion is dear to me. //19//
Madhusūdana: Furthermore, regarding the word "equal" (*sama*):
this is an elaboration of the preceding point.
"Free from attachment" means being devoid of the superimposition of attractiveness upon all objects, whether sentient or insentient.
The meaning is that he is always devoid of joy and dejection; this is clear. //18//
Furthermore, "equal in blame and praise" means that blame is the recounting of faults,
while praise is the recounting of virtues.
He for whom [all things] are equal because they produce neither suffering nor pleasure is such [a person].

He is a sage (*maunī*), one whose speech is restrained. To the objection that activity of speech is indeed necessary for the maintenance of the body's existence, he replies: "Contented," meaning one whose desire has ceased.
Furthermore: one who is homeless, meaning devoid of a fixed dwelling;
