one whose mind is steady, meaning whose intellect is fixed upon the ultimate reality as its object—such a devoted person is dear to Me.
Furthermore, devotion is mentioned here again and again in order to establish that devotion alone is the sufficient cause for liberation. //19//
Viśvanātha: "Homeless" (aniketa) means one who is devoid of attachment to his own natural abode. //18-19//
Baladeva: "Equal toward an enemy" has a clear meaning. "Free from attachment" means devoid of bad association (*kusaṅga*).
"Alike," he who does not experience pain through censure nor pleasure through praise.
He is silent, restrained in speech, or habituated to reflecting on his own desired [truth];
satisfied with any food, whether harsh or pleasant, obtained by chance and unseen;
homeless, devoid of a fixed dwelling, or empty of the delusion regarding a home.
"Steadfast-minded" means one whose knowledge is certain.
Regarding these seven qualities beginning with "he who is without hatred," the fact that they are mentioned again is not a fault, as it is intended to demonstrate their extreme rarity.

These attributes, such as being without hatred and so forth, which exist together in the three types of devotees—beginning with those established in goodness (sāttvika)—should be reconciled by the wise according to their respective degrees of possibility. (18–19)
But those who worship this immortal nectar of dharma as it has been described, full of faith, regarding Me as their supreme goal— they, being devotees, are exceedingly dear to Me. 12.20
Śrīdhara: With the words "But those who... (ye tu), he concludes the exposition of the various categories of dharma along with their fruits. "As stated" means in the manner previously described.
Dharma itself is the nectar (amṛta).
Because it is the means for attaining immortality (*amṛtatva*),
some read the word as *dharmyamṛtam*. Those who worship— that is, practice— it while exercising faith.
And those who, being devoted to Me, are My devotees—they are exceedingly dear to Me. //20//
Since the path of the unmanifest is indeed full of suffering and many obstacles, the wise person,
possessing the true path of devotion, should worship the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa for the sake of happiness.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Devotion Yoga," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī. //12//
Madhusūdana:

By the passage beginning with "adveṣṭā" (one who is not hateful), the collection of dharmas that constitute the innate nature and serve as the characteristics of the renunciants who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and who worship the Imperishable (*akṣara*) has been described.
As it is stated in the *Vārttika*:
"For one who has realized the Self, qualities such as being non-hostile arise spontaneously and do not take the form of deliberate means.
This very point was previously stated in the form of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established.
Demonstrating that this collection of teachings, when accomplished with effort, becomes the means to liberation for one seeking liberation, he concludes with the words "But those who...

Those renunciants seeking liberation who fully attend to— that is, practice— the nectar of dharma (dharma-amṛta), which is called "nectar" because it is a means to nectar and because it is as delicious as nectar, namely this Veda as set forth beginning with "He who is not hateful toward any being," and so on.

Those who, with effort and faith, being virtuous, hold Me as their supreme goal— meaning those devotees for whom I, the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the imperishable Self, am the only supreme object to be attained and the unsurpassed refuge— and who thus worship Me as the unconditioned Brahman, they are exceedingly dear to Me.
"This is the conclusion of what was previously indicated by the statement: 'For I am exceedingly dear to the knower, and he is dear to Me.

Since one who practices this nectar of dharma with faith becomes exceedingly dear to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Controller, therefore this [devotion] is both the natural characteristic of the possessor of knowledge and, for the seeker of liberation who desires to know the reality of the Self, a means to the knowledge of the Self."

The meaning of the statement is that this must be practiced with effort by one desiring to go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Thus, for the primary qualified aspirant— characterized by qualities such as non-enmity— who, through the ripening of meditation upon Brahman with attributes (*sopādhika-brahmābhidhyāna*), contemplates Brahman without attributes (*nirupādhika-brahmānusandadhāna*) and repeatedly practices hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the true nature of the meaning of the Vedānta texts becomes possible.

Therefore, for the sake of attaining liberation, the referent of the word "That" (tat-padartha)—which is capable of being connected with the meaning of the great Vedāntic mahāvākya that is the cause of liberation—must be investigated; this is established by the middle group of six [chapters]. //20//

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Devotion," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā-gūḍhārtha-dīpikā* (The Lamp Illuminating the Hidden Meaning of the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā), composed by the venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.
Viśvanātha said:

Concluding the various duties rooted in devotion to his own devotees, he states the fruit of hearing and reflecting upon these [teachings] for those who desire them in their entirety with the words "But those...
These qualities arising from devotion and arising from peace are not material *guṇas*, because of the maxim stated elsewhere: "Kṛṣṇa is pleased by devotion, but not by the *guṇas*."

However, those who have been described by the aforementioned definitions as being devoted (bhakta) are established in the excellent nature of each [individual] separately. But these [others], desiring all the various existing characteristics, are practitioners (sādhaka); they are superior even to those who are perfected (siddha).
For this very reason, there is the word "exceedingly" (ati). //20//

Devotion alone, possessing wonderful qualities, is the most excellent of all, consisting of bliss, and the perfect accomplisher of all that is to be achieved; thus has the meaning of this chapter been set forth.
Although knowledge and devotion are shown to be like the nimba fruit and the grape, nevertheless,
these two are taken up by those who crave their respective flavors.
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary that showers the essence of meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, the twelfth chapter of the *Gītā* has been properly concluded for the virtuous. 12.
Baladeva: Concluding the aforementioned yoga of devotion, He states the fruit of steadfastness in that [devotion] with the words "But those who...
Those devotees who, having fixed their minds on Me as previously described in such passages as "those who, fixing their minds on Me," etc., practice this nectar of dharma as it has been presented;
they take refuge in that [dharma] just as they would in Me, the goal to be attained, for it is the means of attainment.
Those who are full of faith, possessing even a small atom of devotion and faith, who regard Me as the Supreme and delight in Me—they become exceedingly dear to Me. //20//

The glorious Kṛṣṇa is under the control of those who enjoy Him alone; however, He is even more intensely under the control of those who enjoy Him through exclusive devotion, for He is moved by their love alone—such is the determination of the twelve [verses].
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.
